detailed_rationale:
Schloss Bangalore (The Leela Palaces, Hotels & Resorts) is India's premier domestic luxury hotel chain, which completed India's largest-ever hospitality IPO in May-June 2025 (oversubscribed 4.7x). The IPO was explicitly structured to deleverage the balance sheet: total borrowings fell from Rs 4,242 crore (FY24) to Rs 3,909 crore (FY25), and net debt was cut further in FY26 from Rs 25,677 million to Rs 12,707 million - a roughly Rs 1,297 crore reduction in a single year. This deleveraging directly shows up in the P&L: Q1 FY26 interest cost fell to Rs 86 crore from Rs 119 crore a year earlier, and the company swung from a Rs 75 crore loss to a Rs 9 crore profit in the same quarter. FY25 itself was the company's first profitable year (Rs 47.66 crore) after two years of losses, on revenue that grew from Rs 903 crore (FY23) to Rs 1,407 crore (FY25).

The quant panel's ROE of only 3.82% looks like a red flag in isolation but is a direct artifact of this history, not a sign of a weak business: the company only turned profitable in FY25, the IPO enlarged the equity base substantially (primary proceeds used mostly for debt paydown rather than compounding retained earnings), and net income is still ramping from a low base while ROCE (19.55%) - which better isolates asset-level earning power ahead of the capital-structure changes - is already healthy. This is a genuine business inflection, not stale data, and the ROE metric should mechanically improve over the next several years as (a) interest expense keeps falling with further deleveraging and (b) operating leverage plays out on rising occupancy/ADR.

Operating momentum is real: Q1 FY26 revenue grew 17% to Rs 275 crore with EBITDA up 39% to Rs 101 crore (37% margin, up from 31%); Q2 FY26 revenue grew 11% to Rs 333 crore with RevPAR up 13% to Rs 13,262 and occupancy at 69%. Management has guided mid-to-high-teens EBITDA growth for FY26 and set an ambitious FY30 EBITDA target above Rs 2,000 crore - a target that implies a very steep multi-year CAGR from the current EBITDA base and almost certainly assumes meaningful new-key/inventory additions on top of same-store RevPAR gains, so it should be read as a management aspiration rather than a base-rate expectation. India's luxury hospitality segment is in a genuine structural upcycle (rising business and leisure travel, MICE demand, and constrained luxury room-supply growth nationally giving incumbents like Leela real pricing power), which supports the RevPAR/ADR trends seen so far.
recommendation_rationale: Quant scores this a Hold on both windows (54.1 / 54.8), and the story - a newly-delevered, newly-profitable luxury hotel operator riding a genuine India luxury-travel upcycle - is a Hold rather than a rescue-from-Sell or an escalation candidate: fundamentals are inflecting the right way, but the still-low ROE, the ambitious (not yet proven) FY30 target, and a rich-ish multiple on an early-innings earnings base argue against reading this as anything stronger than Hold today.
summary: The Leela's owner, Schloss Bangalore, used India's largest-ever hotel IPO in 2025 to pay down a large chunk of debt, and the numbers since have moved the right way - revenue and EBITDA both growing at double-digit rates, interest costs falling, and the company profitable for the first time after two loss-making years. The very low return-on-equity figure in our data reflects that recent history (new equity base, still-ramping profit) rather than a weak business - asset-level returns (ROCE) are already healthy. India's luxury hotel segment is in a strong up-cycle, which is helping room rates and occupancy. This is a story still proving itself post-IPO rather than a name with an established earnings track record, so we rate it a Hold.
positive_para: Aggressive, IPO-funded deleveraging (net debt roughly halved in FY26) is directly cutting interest expense and driving the swing to profitability; genuine operating momentum (Q1 FY26 EBITDA +39%, margin 31%->37%; Q2 FY26 RevPAR +13%, occupancy 69%); ROCE of ~19.6% shows the underlying hotel assets already earn healthy returns even before the capital structure fully normalizes; India's luxury/upscale hospitality segment benefits from constrained new luxury room supply and rising business/leisure/MICE travel, giving incumbents real pricing power; management has a credible, well-capitalized long-term growth ambition (FY30 EBITDA target).
negative_para: ROE of only ~3.8% - even allowing for the post-IPO/turnaround context - means the company has not yet demonstrated it can sustainably compound on its enlarged equity base; the FY30 EBITDA target (>Rs 2,000 crore) implies a very steep multi-year ramp that almost certainly depends on new hotel/key additions executing on time and on budget, which is unproven; interest coverage of ~3.65x, while improving, is still only moderate for a company whose core asset (real estate-heavy luxury hotels) carries meaningful residual debt; a PE near 40x prices in a good deal of the turnaround already succeeding, leaving limited room for a demand shock (travel is discretionary and macro-sensitive) or execution slippage on new properties.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~40x trailing earnings on a still-small, only-recently-positive profit base, the multiple is effectively pricing the next several years of the turnaround - continued deleveraging, occupancy/ADR gains, and successful execution of new luxury inventory - rather than today's actual return ratios (ROE ~3.8%). If the deleveraging and RevPAR trends continue as they have in the last two quarters, the ROE trajectory should improve meaningfully over 2-3 years and could justify the multiple in hindsight; if the FY30 EBITDA ambition proves overly aggressive or a demand downturn hits discretionary luxury travel, today's price offers little margin of safety. Call it fair-to-rich, priced for continued successful execution rather than for today's balance sheet.
